content: In Niigata Prefecture, 690 individuals from the Agano River basin were officially recognized as patients suffering from Niigata Minamata disease. This condition, caused by organic mercury poisoning, was the second recorded outbreak of Minamata disease in Japan, following the initial incident in Kumamoto Prefecture. Due to its location in the Lower Agano River Basin, it is sometimes referred to as Niigata Minamata disease or Agano River Minamata disease. It is one of the Four Big Pollution Diseases of Japan. From the autumn of 1964 to the spring of 1965, unusual behavior was observed in cats living along the Agano River. These animals exhibited symptoms such as dilated pupils, excessive salivation, convulsions, and erratic behavior, often culminating in death. For instance, one cat reportedly ran into a clay cooking stove containing burning charcoal, convulsed, and died after emitting a strange cry. These alarming symptoms were soon observed in humans as well. In April and May 1965, Professor Tadao Tsubaki of Niigata University examined two patients and suspected Minamata disease. Analysis of one patient’s hair revealed a mercury concentration of 390 parts per million (ppm). On May 31, 1965, Professor Tsubaki reported an outbreak of organic mercury poisoning in the Agano River basin to the prefectural government, and his findings were made public on June 12. The investigation into the Niigata outbreak benefited from the experience gained during the original Minamata incident. Researchers from the Kumamoto University Research Group, which had studied the first outbreak, and Dr. Hajime Hosokawa, the former director of Chisso Hospital, applied their expertise to the Niigata case. Unlike the initial Minamata investigation, the Niigata inquiry progressed more efficiently due to collaboration among the prefectural government, Niigata University, citizen organizations, and local residents. By March 1966, factory wastewater was identified as a potential source of the pollution. In September 1966, the Ministry of Health and Welfare confirmed the presence of methylmercury in moss samples collected near the wastewater outlet of the Showa Denko factory in Kanose village. Showa Denko, the company implicated in the Niigata outbreak, responded in a manner similar to Chisso Corporation during the original Minamata incident. The company attempted to discredit the researchers and proposed alternative explanations for the disease. Showa Denko distributed informational leaflets denying that their wastewater was the cause and suggested that agricultural chemical runoff, possibly triggered by the 1964 Niigata earthquake, might be responsible. Unlike the victims in Minamata, the Niigata patients lived far from the factory and had no direct ties to Showa Denko. This geographical and social distance fostered greater community support for the affected individuals. In March 1968, a lawsuit was filed against Showa Denko, just three years after the outbreak was made public. This was in stark contrast to the Minamata case, where the first lawsuit was filed 13 years after the initial outbreak. On September 26, 1968, the government released an official report concluding that the mercury poisoning was likely caused by prolonged discharge of mercury from the Kanose plant. However, the report did not entirely exclude other potential causes. Showa Denko’s president, Masao Yasunishi, continued to deny the company’s responsibility. The Niigata lawsuit ultimately succeeded. On September 29, 1971, the court found Showa Denko guilty of negligence. Compensation was awarded to the victims: A family member of a deceased patient testified in court, describing the harrowing experience: My father was crazed like a wild beast and then died—agonized, in pain like a dog. The events in Niigata had a profound impact on the response to the original Minamata incident. The scientific research conducted in Niigata prompted a re-evaluation of earlier studies in Minamata. Furthermore, the decision of Niigata patients to pursue legal action against the polluting company inspired similar efforts in Minamata. Masazumi Harada, a prominent researcher, remarked, It may sound strange, but if this second Minamata disease had not broken out, the medical and social progress achieved by now in Kumamoto would have been impossible.
